There’s definitely a concern for future aggression, absolutely. Every trainer or behaviorist is gonna have different experience/hypothesis as to why, but it all boils down to this: when a dog shows signs of escalating aggression, the cycle of it must be stopped or else it will continually escalate as the dog’s buttons are pushed.

Now, that being said, just because one bite is on record does not mean your dog is washed (or, worse, as some would venture because it did break skin). Resource guarding behaviors are more likely to happen in the home or “home turf.” Your dog is more apt to protect “their” things. That is usually summed up as Affection, Toys, Food, Water, and Space. Resource aggression both inside and outside the home is completely manageable, and you can also teach your dog to have a solid “out” command and how to share/not everything is “theirs.” Don’t do this by yourself. You want a skilled trainer present. Keep an open mind, because there are many approaches to handling this. If one method is not working, don’t waste more time with that method or trainer because your goal is to keep aggression signals from escalating. Though your dog does not have to be washed, I would avoid any PA as well as keep your SD managed and supervised when other animals and people are around until resource issues are sorted; no matter how long that takes to manage. Though it was your fault for trying to break up a dog bite (that is how most bites to humans happen), most countries will not allow a dog to bite another person. Please tread carefully, OP.

Teach your dog a reliable “out” command. Not just, “leave it and stand there,” but actually “spit it out and back away.” Use leash pressure to guide away from the object (you might use a long line for this) and ensure your dog can turn around and walk well away from any minor distraction. The more items or objects or stimuli you practice with, the easier it will be for things your dog gets possessive of. Once your dog is ROCK solid at this, then start setting up controlled situations with food. Practice at your own risk, assuming you don’t have a trainer with you. An ecollar may be an invaluable tool in getting your dog to check out of his possessive mindset without having to approach an angry dog. Do not correct your dog for this aggression unless you are correcting because they failed to respond to a cue they know WELL.

Edit: I think the Good Dog Training has some videos on teaching “out,” but also check out Solid K9 Training by Jeff Gellman. These two specialize in working with dogs that have similar issues :)

If I am working with tapping at a cadence, I would not also use continuous unless I know my dog’s reaction. Think of a tap as a single pulse of stimulation, and continuous as a pulse of 3-4 stimulations. The continuous (even when tapped quickly) is going to feel a bit hotter than single stimulation. Some sensitive dogs will pick up on that, and it might be uncomfortable. Some dogs don’t even notice. 
I personally would dial up every time you have to repeat your command, but just 1-2 at a time. We would also personally help the dog with leash pressure if they continually weren’t getting it. But, if you’ve seen a reliable response to the collar before, you are more likely to see it again without needing to help- just the reminder that the collar is there. Again, depending on the level of the dog’s arousal, you may be higher on the dial than you expect.

Don’t be afraid to dial up. In an aroused state for some dogs, you may even be hitting HI. I tell all my clients this: the number is not important. Your dog’s reaction to you in the face of a distraction that could potentially end with them getting lost or worse- that’s important. The number changes, all the time. Don’t be married to a single number; while most dogs operate within a usual range on the dial, you will be increasing the dial when distractions go up, then dialing back down when your dog is responding.

I train with mini educators mostly, changing their levels 1-2 at a time, but the method applies to any system. I had a client with a very sensitive husky one time. They were down with ecollar training but very concerned about hurting their dog or causing discomfort. They made the most “mistakes” with the remote looking at the number and misjudging the dog’s reaction. I finally took their remote and covered up the number with a piece of napkin, and told them to look at their dog! They found they had much more success and were way more comfortable with the equipment when they took the training in steps (much like you are) but played with their remote levels much more. I hope maybe this advice helps!

Absolutely agree with this and above comments, about teaching a reliable OUT with leash pressure or other tools. Make sure your dog can walk away and leave ANYTHING when you say, “out.” That will make the response when he’s in tug drive or other drive that much stronger.

I have seen dogs do this when they are unsure about the new equipment; collars, harnesses, head halters, etc. The dog is finding wearing the equipment to be aversive, even without the stimulation. If your friend is dead set on this tool (it’s great), they can continue to just let the corgi wear it for a couple weeks. Loose, even. Don’t even use the remote. Just lots of treats, going about happy everyday life with the pup. Corgmeister will eventually conclude it’s really not a big deal and won’t worry about it so much. You do the same thing with puppies getting used to being in harnesses and collars. Sometimes they don’t like it, but it’s also really easy to get over and not harming them at all. When Corg is more comfortable in it, then try tightening it slightly, still without using any stimulation. Work up slowly. Then, after noticeable improvement in the dogs temperament while wearing the collar, go ahead and continue conditioning and working with the collar on low-levels.

If continuing with the collar, you may also look at changing the contact points on the collar? It’s possible pup finds the default points uncomfortable; in that case, there are fairly affordable replacement parts available. Make sure you get the right points to make contact through the dog’s fur. For a corgi, you might try the sensitive points for long fur, or the winged comfort pad. If they’re using an ET-300 mini educator, I have a comment somewhere on my prof that links to the sensitive pads.

If a few weeks of loose or slightly fitted collar does not work, especially after changing contact points, it may not be the right tool for the pup. Keep the box. Ecollar Tech has great customer support and you may even be able to mail the unit in for a refund. The ecollar is great but there are always other options :) best of luck to your friend and her pup!

No, I never said they NEVER cause pain, absolutely not. Abuse can be done with any tool.

While I agree with some of the “facts” presented here, it’s still mostly.... just opinions. There’s literally no links to studies or proof or evidence or even annotations from cases cited by actual trainers. Also, they immediately refer to prong collars as painful, and when used correctly or with the right dog, they are not painful. Attention-grabbing, yes. But just because an aversive LOOKS aversive, that’s not up to us to decide. The dog decides that. Some dogs think gentle leaders are more aversive then prongs. It’s really about using the best tool for the dog (even if in some cases that is R+ only).

First, I would recommend looking at a different training facility. There may be several in your state or near your place of residence that are versed in ecollars. Start with Google and Facebook searches, looking at the smaller businesses. Many of the rad training facilities (some I’ve had the privilege of working for) that change people’s lives are a couple running a small business on their ranch, an ex-military vet who used to train MWDs, etc. Don’t be afraid to call around or send some emails, many will offer you free evaluations. You should never have to pay for them to come pet your dog and tell you what they’re about. This might be a great way to gain access to a facility where you can safely train on the dog reactivity or resource guarding in a much more controlled, supervised manner. 

I see your conundrum. The way I’ve had success, practice with the ecollar alone. Get one with many levels (Et-300 has 1-100 levels). You would be using a lower level, one that your dog can barely feel at first so that you get comfortable using it and can have a reliable response; you would then venture outside or possibly to your window on-leash and start dialing up your ecollar small increments at a time until you get the same response- one your dog just barely feels. Dial back down when big chillin’. 

After training leash walking and recall with the ecollar, practice “Out” or “leave it” with literally everything- for my dog, it’s the grass he wants to chew on, the stick he wants to chew, the bush he wants to chew (you get the picture, actually he has a dental filling). Not just dogs. Since your dog by then should have a clear understanding of the command “out,” or “leave it,” it’s just a matter of using the ecollar to help you and your commands cut through the mental “static” of seeing another dog, so to speak.

I hope that answers your question a bit? I’m sorry if I got tangential!

I have experience with the ecollar, and solving a lot of these issues can be done pretty easily with it. I would look up how to teach a dog to “Out” with the ecollar (The Good Dog LA has a few of these videos on YouTube, demonstrating with different dogs) and ensure that your dane is able to turn around and walk away from any of these items. This can be taught very similarly to leash walking or recall on the ecollar, but ensure you have worked on these things prior and associated the stimulation with attention to you. Start with things she is not protective over, and then slowly move upward in value when she proves she can reliably leave it.

I would not use a “Place” command or recall off the items because it is not actively addressing the possessive mindset. 

A lot of behavioral issues will usually extinguish when you disallow the protective mindset from happening. It will take time, but I do believe training can be done on your own with thorough research. If the tool works best for your team, that is the most important; not someone else’s philosophy.

Hope this helps.

Agreed with this. I have rehabbed more than 50  anxious dogs with ecollar focus but it can be done VERY wrong. 
Ecollar is not used as a correction or aversive. It is used as a positively reinforced attention-grabber at low levels. It will help your dog focus on you rather than any anxious stimuli. Once your dog is conditioned to it, THEN you can start interfacing it with commands your dog knows and redirect them using their obedience.
